case_analysis.focal_point: Whether California’s Proposition 12—which conditions in-state sales of pork on compliance with certain animal-confinement standards—violates the dormant Commerce Clause by impermissibly regulating or burdening interstate commerce (including by effectively controlling out-of-state production practices).
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Constitution, Article I, Section 8, Clause 3 (Commerce Clause) as construed through the dormant Commerce Clause doctrine; related framework includes Pike v. Bruce Church balancing (undue burden on interstate commerce).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners (national pork producers and farm interests) argue Proposition 12 is an unconstitutional extraterritorial and/or undue burdening regulation because California is using its market power to force producers nationwide to change farming practices occurring wholly outside California as a condition of accessing California’s consumer market. They contend the law imposes substantial compliance and restructuring costs across the national pork supply chain, with minimal or speculative in-state benefits, and therefore fails dormant Commerce Clause scrutiny—either because it effectively regulates out-of-state conduct or because it places burdens on interstate commerce that are clearly excessive in relation to local benefits under Pike balancing.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents (California officials) argue Proposition 12 is a valid in-state sales regulation that applies evenhandedly to all pork sold in California regardless of origin, does not directly regulate out-of-state commerce, and serves legitimate state interests (e.g., animal welfare and asserted health/safety interests). They further argue that petitioners’ characterization of the law’s effects is overstated or inconsistent with industry realities and that, under Ninth Circuit doctrine, the measure does not trigger invalid extraterritoriality and should survive Pike because the state’s interests justify any incidental interstate burdens.
key_precedents: Association des Eleveurs de Canards et d’Oies du Quebec v. Harris (9th Cir. 2013)
National Pork Producers Council v. Ross (2023)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Alito is right to press that, if we deem large upstream compliance costs categorically irrelevant, Pike risks becoming a dead letter and big States could effectively set national standards. But as Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, our “extraterritoriality” precedents have been confined to price-control/price-affirmation regimes, and Proposition 12 is instead an evenhanded condition on in-state sales—precisely the sort of product standard that often has spillover effects without triggering a per se rule. National Pork Producers reinforces the institutional concern that courts are not equipped to perform open-ended cost–benefit review, especially where the asserted “benefits” include moral and welfare judgments that legislatures commonly make; on this record, it is hard to say the burdens are “clearly excessive” without converting Pike into freewheeling policy supervision. A narrow disposition rejecting an expanded extraterritoriality theory while leaving room for a better-developed Pike showing in a different case best fits precedent and preserves institutional legitimacy.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Alito’s Pike-centered argument—that California’s market power effectively coerces nationwide production and invites balkanization—raises a serious policy concern, but it depends on an atextual judicial authority to invalidate evenhanded state sales conditions by weighing speculative economic burdens against moral or welfare interests. As Justice Gorsuch emphasizes, that balancing enterprise lacks administrable, constitutionally grounded standards and risks turning courts into economic regulators, especially where the law governs only in-state sales and any upstream restructuring follows from private choices to access California’s market. Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s reliance on our confinement of “extraterritoriality” to price-control/price-affirmation regimes reinforces that downstream effects alone do not convert an in-state product standard into direct regulation of out-of-state commerce. Absent discrimination or a conflicting federal statute, the structural concerns Alito identifies are for Congress to address under the Commerce Clause, not for this Court to police through expanded dormant Commerce Clause doctrine.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan are right that our per se “extraterritoriality” cases largely involve price-control/price-affirmation regimes, so I do not rest on a categorical theory. But Justice Gorsuch’s administrability objection, while serious, cannot justify treating major, foreseeable out-of-state restructuring costs as effectively “noncognizable,” because that would drain Pike of meaningful content whenever a State drafts its rule as an in-state sales condition. Unlike the modest upstream effects in Clover Leaf, petitioners plausibly allege that California’s market power predictably compels nationwide production changes, the sort of structural spillover the Commerce Clause was designed to prevent. National Pork Producers counsels against freewheeling balancing, but it does not require dismissal at the pleading stage where burdens of this magnitude could plausibly be found clearly excessive relative to asserted interests that are largely moral and not tied to concrete in-state health or safety gains.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Alito’s Pike argument most directly challenges my view: that California’s market power and predictable nationwide restructuring costs risk balkanization even without discrimination. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, our extraterritoriality cases are cabined to price-control/price-affirmation regimes, and treating ordinary in-state product standards as per se unconstitutional because supply chains adjust would endanger a wide range of consumer-protection laws. Under Pike, the relevant question is not whether compliance costs are large, but whether they are clearly excessive relative to legitimate local interests; I do not accept, as Alito suggests, that animal-welfare and consumer choice interests are categorically “noncognizable,” and Justice Gorsuch is right that courts lack administrable metrics to second-guess those judgments on this record. Absent discrimination or a conflicting federal enactment, I remain unconvinced we have a principled basis to override California’s democratic decision merely because its market share makes compliance influential nationwide.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Alito is right to warn that Pike cannot be nullified by deeming large out-of-state compliance costs categorically “noncognizable,” but I do not read the Ninth Circuit (or our precedents) as adopting that categorical rule; rather, the problem is that the complaint’s cost allegations, without a workable way to measure and compare them against California’s asserted interests, do not plausibly meet Pike’s demanding “clearly excessive” standard. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, upstream supply-chain adjustments are a routine consequence of evenhanded in-state sales standards, and our extraterritoriality line has been confined to price-control/price-affirmation regimes—so converting market-power “spillovers” into a constitutional defect would destabilize ordinary product regulation. Justice Gorsuch’s administrability point reinforces that a broader Pike theory here would invite freewheeling judicial second-guessing of policy tradeoffs, exactly what National Pork Producers cautioned against. If there is a national balkanization problem from divergent animal-welfare standards, Congress has the tools to address it; expanding dormant Commerce Clause invalidation beyond discrimination or a truly clear excess is not doctrinally coherent.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Alito’s Pike argument most directly presses the risk of balkanization when a large State’s market power induces nationwide production changes, but it still depends on courts performing a kind of cost-benefit appraisal—especially of moral or welfare interests—that our doctrine has never rendered administrable without drifting into policymaking. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, our “extraterritoriality” line is cabined to price-control/price-affirmation regimes; extending it to any evenhanded in-state sales condition with upstream effects would constitutionalize a broad limit lacking textual and historical grounding. Justice Thomas’s skepticism of Pike reinforces the separation-of-powers problem: absent discrimination or federal preemption, the Constitution leaves these tradeoffs to Congress and state electorates, not federal judges. On this record, Proposition 12 regulates only in-state sales, and any out-of-state restructuring is a private response to market access, not a direct command to regulate commerce wholly outside California.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Alito’s Pike-focused point most directly presses my concerns: if large out-of-state compliance costs are always treated as “noncognizable,” Pike risks becoming toothless. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, our extraterritoriality line is historically confined to price-control/price-affirmation regimes, and Proposition 12 is an evenhanded in-state sales condition whose upstream effects resemble the ordinary ripple effects recognized in cases like Clover Leaf and reaffirmed in National Pork Producers. Under Pike, I do not see an administrable, precedent-grounded way on this record to declare California’s asserted consumer/animal-welfare interests categorically illegitimate or to conclude the alleged burdens are clearly excessive without converting judicial review into open-ended economic policymaking—an institutional role our recent guidance cautions against. Alito’s structural balkanization concern is serious, but in our system it is primarily addressed through Congress’s commerce power, not by expanding dormant Commerce Clause invalidation beyond discrimination or a clearly excessive burden shown with a developed record.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point—that California’s market power effectively pressures nationwide production changes and that Pike must retain teeth—does not, on a textualist and precedent-bound view, justify extending dormant Commerce Clause invalidation beyond discrimination or the narrow price-control “extraterritoriality” line. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, our extraterritoriality cases are best read as confined to price-affirmation/price-control regimes, and treating ordinary, evenhanded in-state sales standards as per se invalid would destabilize a wide range of product regulations with inevitable upstream effects. On Pike, I agree with Justice Gorsuch that courts lack administrable, principled metrics to deem asserted animal-welfare (or related consumer) interests categorically “noncognizable” or to conclude—on this record—that the burdens are “clearly excessive,” particularly where producers remain free to sell noncompliant products outside California. Alito’s balkanization concern is structurally serious, but under our precedents the more legitimate remedy is congressional action, not judicially expanding Pike into open-ended economic and moral policymaking.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Alito’s best point is that Pike must retain some force and that a large State can, in practice, induce nationwide production changes through an in-state sales condition. But as Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch stress, our precedents (including Clover Leaf and National Pork Producers) caution against converting Pike into open-ended economic policymaking, especially where the challenged law is evenhanded and regulates only what may be sold in the State. The alleged “coercion” here largely reflects private supply-chain choices to serve California’s market, and petitioners have not shown—on this record—that the incidental burdens are clearly excessive relative to California’s legitimate interests in the characteristics of products sold to its consumers, even if those interests include nonquantifiable welfare concerns. Chief Justice Roberts’s emphasis on cabining extraterritoriality to price-control/price-affirmation regimes reinforces that the proper posture is skepticism toward categorical invalidation and caution in balancing absent discrimination or a truly clear excess.

John Roberts.reasoning: Proposition 12 regulates only the in-state sale of pork and applies evenhandedly to in-state and out-of-state producers, so it does not amount to the kind of discrimination or direct regulation of wholly out-of-state commerce the dormant Commerce Clause forbids under Article I, § 8, cl. 3. Petitioners’ complaint that compliance will require upstream changes outside California is appropriately assessed, if at all, under Pike v. Bruce Church’s undue-burden balancing rather than an expansive “extraterritoriality” theory, consistent with this Court’s approach to similar upstream-effects laws (e.g., Minnesota v. Clover Leaf Creamery). On this record, the asserted burdens largely reflect market choices by private actors to access California’s market, while California asserts nontrivial local interests, making it difficult to say the burdens are “clearly excessive” in relation to the putative benefits under Pike. A narrow holding rejecting a broad extraterritoriality rule and declining to invalidate a nondiscriminatory sales condition better preserves federalism and institutional legitimacy by avoiding a sweeping reworking of dormant Commerce Clause doctrine.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Article I, §8, cl. 3 grants Congress—not this Court—a freestanding power to regulate interstate commerce, and the so-called dormant Commerce Clause (especially Pike v. Bruce Church balancing) lacks a firm footing in the Constitution’s text and original public meaning. Proposition 12 is an evenhanded condition on in-state sales, not a facial discrimination against interstate commerce or a tariff-like barrier, and any downstream effects on out-of-state production do not convert a sales rule into an impermissible extraterritorial regulation. To the extent Pike invites courts to weigh “burdens” against “benefits,” it is an atextual invitation to policy-making that should not be used to invalidate a state law regulating products sold within the State absent clear discrimination or a conflicting federal statute. Consistent with National Pork Producers Council v. Ross (2023), I would uphold Proposition 12 against this dormant Commerce Clause challenge.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Proposition 12 is a facially nondiscriminatory in-state sales condition, but under Pike v. Bruce Church, Inc. it is unconstitutional if it imposes burdens on interstate commerce that are clearly excessive in relation to the putative local benefits. Petitioners plausibly allege that California is leveraging its market power to force costly changes in out-of-state production practices across a national supply chain, with benefits that are, at best, difficult to substantiate and largely moral or policy-driven rather than tied to concrete in-state health or safety gains. Accepting the Ninth Circuit’s approach that large compliance and restructuring costs borne primarily out of state are “noncognizable” would drain Pike balancing of meaningful content and invite States to regulate national markets indirectly through sales bans. The Commerce Clause’s structural purpose is to prevent precisely this sort of balkanizing, coercive spillover regulation, and Pike supplies the appropriate tool to invalidate it here.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Proposition 12 regulates only in-state sales and applies evenhandedly to all pork sold in California, regardless of origin, placing it within the State’s traditional police powers rather than constituting a per se invalid “extraterritorial” regulation under the dormant Commerce Clause (U.S. Const. art. I, § 8, cl. 3). Under Pike v. Bruce Church, Inc., 397 U.S. 137 (1970), the asserted burdens are largely compliance costs associated with accessing California’s market, and petitioners have not shown those incidental effects on interstate commerce are “clearly excessive” in relation to California’s putative interests in animal-welfare and related health/safety concerns. The Court should be wary of using Pike to invalidate democratically enacted, nondiscriminatory consumer-product standards based on contested predictions about national supply-chain adjustments, particularly where the law does not facially discriminate and leaves producers free to sell noncompliant products elsewhere. Consistent with National Pork Producers Council v. Ross (2023), the dormant Commerce Clause does not provide a roving mandate to strike down state sales regulations simply because they influence out-of-state production decisions.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Proposition 12 is an evenhanded in-state sales condition that applies to all pork sold in California regardless of origin, so it is not a facially discriminatory tariff-like measure and does not fit the narrow “extraterritoriality” line reserved for price-control and price-affirmation statutes. Under Pike v. Bruce Church, the asserted burdens—costly supply-chain adjustments with significant out-of-state ripple effects—do not alone establish a dormant Commerce Clause violation absent a showing that those burdens are clearly excessive in relation to California’s putative local benefits, which include consumer/market regulation and the State’s asserted health and moral interests tied to products sold within its borders. National Pork Producers Council v. Ross confirms that courts should be cautious about turning Pike into a roving inquiry into policy wisdom or nationwide economic integration, especially where the law regulates only in-state sales and leaves producers free to sell noncompliant products elsewhere. On this record and framework, petitioners’ allegations of substantial interstate effects do not suffice to invalidate a nondiscriminatory sales restriction under Article I, § 8, cl. 3 as construed through the dormant Commerce Clause.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Article I, §8, cl. 3 empowers Congress to regulate interstate commerce, but the dormant Commerce Clause doctrine should not be extended to invalidate an evenhanded in-state sales condition simply because it induces upstream changes outside the State. Proposition 12 regulates only what may be sold in California and applies without regard to origin; the Court’s “extraterritoriality” cases (e.g., price-control and price-affirmation regimes) do not supply a freestanding rule against laws with out-of-state effects. Under Pike v. Bruce Church, balancing courts are ill-equipped to weigh California’s moral and health-related interests against compliance costs in an integrated national industry, and absent discrimination or a clear congressional command, the Constitution leaves such policy judgments to the political branches. Petitioners’ requested rule would invite federal courts to act as super-legislatures second-guessing state tradeoffs whenever a large State’s consumer market influences production elsewhere.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Proposition 12 is an evenhanded in-state sales condition that applies to all pork sold in California regardless of origin, and it does not facially discriminate against interstate commerce under the Commerce Clause (Art. I, § 8, cl. 3) as construed through the dormant Commerce Clause. Petitioners’ “practical effects” theory sounds in Pike v. Bruce Church balancing rather than a freestanding extraterritoriality rule; as cases like Minnesota v. Clover Leaf Creamery indicate, upstream out-of-state impacts from an in-state sales regulation ordinarily are evaluated under Pike, not treated as categorically invalid. On this record, and consistent with judicial restraint and administrability concerns, courts should be reluctant to invalidate a nondiscriminatory state law by second-guessing contested legislative judgments about animal-welfare-related benefits versus compliance costs, especially where the asserted burdens depend on supply-chain choices by private actors. Absent discrimination or a clearly excessive burden in relation to putative local benefits, precedent and workability counsel upholding the law under Pike.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Proposition 12 regulates only in-state sales of pork and applies evenhandedly to all products sold in California, regardless of origin; on its face it does not discriminate against interstate commerce under the Commerce Clause (U.S. Const. art. I, § 8, cl. 3) as implemented through dormant Commerce Clause doctrine. Petitioners’ “extraterritoriality” theory would convert many ordinary product-standards and sales conditions into per se invalid regulations whenever upstream actors choose to alter out-of-state practices to meet a State’s market requirements, but this Court has treated such indirect practical effects as matters for Pike balancing rather than a freestanding invalidity rule (see Pike v. Bruce Church, 397 U.S. 137 (1970); cf. Clover Leaf Creamery). Under Pike, while compliance costs may be substantial, the judiciary lacks a principled, administrable basis to deem California’s asserted interests in animal welfare and related health/safety concerns “clearly” outweighed on this record, particularly given the presumption that nondiscriminatory regulations with legitimate ends are upheld. Precedent therefore counsels affirmance absent discrimination or a demonstrably excessive burden under Pike, which petitioners have not shown at the requisite level.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Proposition 12 operates as an evenhanded in-state sales condition applicable to all pork sold in California regardless of origin, and the dormant Commerce Clause does not generally bar a State from regulating products within its market simply because doing so influences out-of-state production decisions. Under Pike v. Bruce Church, Inc. (1970), petitioners must plausibly show that the incidental burdens on interstate commerce are clearly excessive in relation to the putative local benefits; here, California’s asserted interests (including animal-welfare and related health/safety concerns) are legitimate, and courts should be cautious about second-guessing and quantifying moral or welfare benefits against compliance-cost allegations at the pleading stage. Consistent with National Pork Producers Council v. Ross (2023), the extraterritoriality principle does not invalidate a nondiscriminatory sales regulation merely due to substantial upstream effects in an integrated national market. Given the absence of discrimination and the difficulty of administrable judicial balancing of contested economic forecasts versus sovereign policy judgments, the dormant Commerce Clause claim should fail.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether California’s Proposition 12, which conditions in-state sale of pork on compliance with specified animal-confinement standards that largely affect out-of-state farming, violates the Dormant Commerce Clause by impermissibly regulating or excessively burdening interstate commerce.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Constitution, Article I, Section 8, Clause 3 (the Commerce Clause) as applied through the Dormant Commerce Clause doctrine; (as discussed by amici) related federal statutory backdrop includes the Animal Health Protection Act, 7 U.S.C. § 8301 et seq., and the Federal Meat Inspection Act, 21 U.S.C. § 601 et seq.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners (national pork and farm trade groups) argue that Proposition 12 effectively forces nationwide changes in hog-raising practices because California is a major market, thereby projecting California’s policy preferences into other States. They contend this is the kind of extraterritorial regulation the Dormant Commerce Clause forbids and, in any event, that the law imposes substantial burdens on interstate commerce that are clearly excessive relative to California’s asserted local interests (animal welfare and related health/safety justifications), warranting invalidation under Dormant Commerce Clause principles (including Pike balancing).
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents (California officials) argue Proposition 12 is a legitimate, evenhanded in-state sales condition that applies to all pork sold in California regardless of origin and does not directly regulate out-of-state conduct. They contend any upstream effects on out-of-state producers are incidental market consequences of California’s choice about what products may be sold within its borders, and that the law serves in-state interests (including public health/safety and moral/consumer concerns about animal confinement), so it should not be struck down under the Dormant Commerce Clause and should survive any balancing test.
key_precedents: Ass’n des Éleveurs de Canards et d’Oies du Québec v. Harris (9th Cir. 2013)
Rocky Mountain Farmers Union v. Corey (9th Cir. 2013)
Food Marketing Institute v. Argus Leader Media (2019)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Alito’s best point is that the complaint plausibly alleges substantial restructuring costs in an integrated national supply chain, and that those allegations deserve to be taken seriously under Pike rather than dismissed as “incidental.” But as Justice Gorsuch emphasizes, our extraterritoriality cases (Healy, Brown-Forman) have been confined to price-control/price-affirmation regimes that directly regulate out-of-state transactions; extending them to neutral in-state sales conditions based on downstream market influence would effectively convert Pike into a per se invalidity rule for many product standards, contrary to Clover Leaf’s treatment of out-of-state impacts through balancing. Justice Kagan’s administrability concern reinforces my minimalist view: at the pleading stage, absent discrimination or direct control of wholly out-of-state commerce, courts should be cautious about invalidating a nondiscriminatory sales regulation by monetizing and discounting asserted health, safety, and moral/consumer interests. On these pleadings, the narrower and more precedent-faithful course is to reject a categorical extraterritoriality theory and to hold petitioners have not shown burdens clearly excessive relative to cognizable in-state interests.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Alito’s best point is that California’s market size can induce nationwide production changes and thus deserves meaningful Pike scrutiny, but that contention depends on a judicially created balancing test with no clear grounding in the Commerce Clause’s original public meaning and invites courts to do policy-laden cost-benefit analysis better left to Congress. As Justice Gorsuch notes, Healy and Brown-Forman involved price-affirmation/price-control schemes that directly regulated out-of-state transactions, whereas Proposition 12 is a neutral condition on in-state sales whose upstream effects flow from private choices to access California’s market. Even taking Pike as precedent, the “clearly excessive” inquiry is too indeterminate here because it would require monetizing disputed compliance-cost projections against California’s asserted health, safety, and moral/consumer interests—an exercise lacking judicially manageable standards. With no discrimination, no direct extraterritorial control of out-of-state commerce, and no clear federal preemption, the Constitution leaves any demand for national uniformity to Congress, not this Court.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch are right that Healy and Brown-Forman involved price-control/price-affirmation laws that directly dictated out-of-state transaction terms, and Proposition 12 is formally an evenhanded in-state sales condition. But as Roberts also acknowledges, California’s market power may force industry-wide restructuring; that allegation, if true, is precisely the kind of substantial interstate burden Pike requires courts to assess rather than dismiss at the threshold as merely an “upstream ripple,” and Clover Leaf confirms Pike—not per se extraterritoriality—is the right framework. Justice Kagan’s administrability concern strengthens, rather than weakens, the need for a meaningful inquiry into whether California’s asserted “benefits” are genuinely tied to in-state health/safety (or otherwise non-illusory) as opposed to exporting moral policy choices nationwide, because without that discipline Pike becomes either empty deference or an invitation to moral projection. Nothing in the FMIA or AHPA provides clear congressional authorization to tolerate a State’s practical national regulation, so the complaint should at least proceed to a real Pike analysis on the alleged burdens and the State’s concrete local interests.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point—that California’s market size effectively pressures a national industry—does not, without more, convert a neutral in-state sales condition into the kind of extraterritorial regulation condemned in Healy and Brown-Forman, which (as Justice Gorsuch stresses) involved direct control over out-of-state pricing/transactions rather than upstream incentives. Taking Alito’s concern seriously still leaves the case in Pike, but at the pleading stage the asserted burdens and compliance-cost projections remain too contested to deem them “clearly excessive” relative to California’s cognizable interests, including consumer protection, health/safety, and moral preferences tied to products sold in-state—an institutional concern Justice Kagan highlights. Treating “practical nationwide influence” as constitutionally suspect would effectively create a per se bar that collapses Pike and threatens many nondiscriminatory product standards, echoing the Chief Justice’s administrability warning. Under my pragmatic approach, absent discrimination, direct out-of-state control, or clear federal preemption, the Constitution leaves this policy choice to California and Congress rather than inviting courts to second-guess it based on uncertain economic forecasts.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Alito’s best point is that California’s market power may drive costly nationwide supply-chain restructuring, and I take seriously his caution that Pike should not be “illusory.” But as Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, our extraterritoriality cases (Healy, Brown-Forman) are aimed at laws that directly regulate out-of-state transactions—especially price-control/price-affirmation regimes—not at evenhanded in-state sales conditions whose upstream effects are mediated by private market choices, as in Clover Leaf Creamery. Under Pike, courts still must ask whether burdens are clearly excessive, and I agree with Justices Sotomayor and Barrett that on these pleadings California’s asserted consumer/health-and-safety (including moral consumer) interests are cognizable and not something we can deem “non-illusory” only by monetizing and ranking them against disputed cost projections. Treating market leverage alone as constitutionally suspect would, as the Chief warns, collapse Pike into a per se rule and substantially expand dormant Commerce Clause doctrine beyond its administrable, anti-discrimination core absent congressional action.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Alito’s best point is that California’s market size may induce nationwide husbandry changes and impose serious compliance costs, but that describes ordinary upstream incentives from an evenhanded in-state sales condition rather than the kind of direct, out-of-state price control condemned in Healy and Brown-Forman. As Chief Justice Roberts notes, treating those practical ripple effects as per se “extraterritoriality” would collapse Pike and constitutionalize a broad swath of state product standards—an expansion our precedents (including Clover Leaf) have not endorsed. Even accepting Pike as binding precedent, I agree with Justice Thomas and Justice Kagan that courts lack a principled, administrable way to declare these burdens “clearly excessive” relative to California’s asserted health, safety, and moral/consumer interests on this record and at this stage. Absent discrimination, direct regulation of wholly out-of-state transactions, or clear federal preemption, the remedy for any felt need for national uniformity lies with Congress, not judicial invalidation under an indeterminate balancing test.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Alito’s best point is that California’s market power may drive nationwide restructuring costs, but that practical influence is not the kind of direct extraterritorial regulation condemned in Healy and Brown-Forman, which (as Justice Gorsuch emphasizes) targeted price-control/price-affirmation schemes dictating out-of-state transaction terms. I agree with Chief Justice Roberts that converting upstream economic ripple effects into a per se constitutional defect would effectively displace Pike and destabilize many nondiscriminatory product standards, pushing courts into open-ended policymaking. Even under Pike, on these pleadings the allegations do not yet show burdens that are “clearly excessive” relative to California’s asserted interests tied to in-state sales, and institutional caution counsels leaving any desire for national uniformity to Congress. Nothing raised in conference identifies discrimination or clear federal preemption that would warrant changing that analysis.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Alito’s best point is that the complaint plausibly alleges large compliance costs and California’s market leverage, so a Pike inquiry should not be dismissed as “incidental” without taking the allegations seriously. But as Justice Gorsuch and the Chief Justice emphasize, our extraterritoriality cases like Healy and Brown-Forman are aimed at laws that directly regulate the terms of out-of-state transactions (especially price-control/affirmation), not neutral in-state sales conditions whose upstream effects follow from private choices to access a market. Converting “practical national influence” into a per se constitutional defect would expand atextual, judge-made doctrine and effectively displace Pike’s already constrained framework, contrary to how cases like Clover Leaf treat out-of-state ripple effects. Given the evenhanded in-state sales rule and the absence of discrimination or clear federal preemption, I remain unpersuaded that the pleadings establish a dormant Commerce Clause violation.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point—that California’s market size can coerce nationwide restructuring—does not, without more, convert a nondiscriminatory in-state sales condition into unconstitutional “extraterritorial” regulation; as Justice Gorsuch explains, our cases like Healy and Brown-Forman condemned price-control/price-affirmation schemes that directly dictated out-of-state transaction terms, which Proposition 12 does not do. I agree with Chief Justice Roberts that treating ordinary upstream ripple effects as per se invalid would effectively collapse Pike and jeopardize many standard product/sales regulations in an integrated national market. On Pike, I remain unpersuaded that courts can or should invalidate this law at the pleading stage by monetizing contested compliance-cost projections against California’s asserted health/safety and consumer-moral interests, especially where the law applies evenhandedly to in- and out-of-state producers. If the burdens are truly intolerable or national uniformity is needed, Congress—and not judicially open-ended dormant Commerce Clause balancing—is the more legitimate and administrable forum for that policy resolution.

John Roberts.reasoning: Proposition 12 is an evenhanded condition on in-state sales that applies regardless of origin and does not, on its face, regulate wholly out-of-state transactions; its upstream effects on out-of-state producers are the sort of “incidental” consequences that Dormant Commerce Clause doctrine typically assesses under Pike v. Bruce Church, Inc., rather than condemning categorically as extraterritorial regulation. Under Pike, a nondiscriminatory statute is upheld unless the burden on interstate commerce is “clearly excessive” in relation to the putative local benefits, and courts should be cautious—both as a matter of administrability and institutional legitimacy—about second-guessing a State’s asserted health, safety, and moral interests in determining what products may be sold within its borders. Petitioners’ broader extraterritoriality theory would risk collapsing Pike by converting substantial practical effects into per se invalidity, contrary to this Court’s approach in cases like Clover Leaf Creamery that treated out-of-state impacts as a subject for balancing rather than automatic invalidation. Nothing in the federal statutory backdrop (including the Federal Meat Inspection Act, 21 U.S.C. § 601 et seq., or the Animal Health Protection Act, 7 U.S.C. § 8301 et seq.) clearly displaces California’s authority to set a neutral in-state sales standard here, so the narrow course is to uphold the law on these pleadings.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Constitution’s text gives Congress—not this Court—authority to regulate commerce “among the several States,” U.S. Const. art. I, § 8, cl. 3, and the so-called Dormant Commerce Clause (especially Pike v. Bruce Church, Inc. balancing) lacks a firm basis in the Commerce Clause’s original public meaning and invites policy-laden judicial second-guessing. Proposition 12 is an evenhanded condition on in-state sales that applies equally to in-state and out-of-state pork and does not purport to regulate conduct outside California’s borders; any upstream effects are incidental consequences of market participation, not unconstitutional “extraterritorial” regulation. Because the law is not discriminatory and the asserted burdens would require courts to engage in the kind of freewheeling cost-benefit analysis Pike encourages, I would not invalidate it on that basis. Nor do the cited federal statutes (e.g., the Federal Meat Inspection Act, 21 U.S.C. § 601 et seq., or the Animal Health Protection Act, 7 U.S.C. § 8301 et seq.) supply a clear textual preemption rule that displaces California’s in-state sales standard here.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Proposition 12 is framed as an evenhanded in-state sales condition, but the practical consequence is to leverage California’s market power to compel costly changes in out-of-state hog-raising practices, functionally projecting California’s regulatory preferences beyond its borders in a way the Dormant Commerce Clause does not tolerate. Even assuming no facial discrimination, the complaint plausibly alleges substantial burdens on interstate commerce—industry-wide restructuring and significant compliance costs—triggering Pike v. Bruce Church balancing, under which a law is invalid if the burdens are clearly excessive in relation to the putative local benefits. Given the attenuated connection between sow-confinement standards and any concrete California health/safety benefit (as opposed to moral preferences), the asserted local benefits appear modest relative to the nationwide burdens, making dismissal without meaningful Pike analysis improper. Nothing in the Animal Health Protection Act, 7 U.S.C. § 8301 et seq., or the Federal Meat Inspection Act, 21 U.S.C. § 601 et seq., supplies a clear congressional authorization for this kind of state-imposed national standard, so ordinary Dormant Commerce Clause limits apply.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Proposition 12 is an evenhanded condition on in-state sales that applies to all pork sold in California regardless of origin, and it does not directly regulate wholly out-of-state transactions in the way the Dormant Commerce Clause’s extraterritoriality cases target. The appropriate framework is Pike v. Bruce Church, Inc. (1970): petitioners must plausibly allege a substantial burden on interstate commerce that is clearly excessive in relation to California’s putative local benefits, including consumer moral concerns and asserted health/safety interests tied to in-state markets. Upstream compliance costs borne by out-of-state producers are largely incidental market consequences of California’s lawful decision about what may be sold within its borders, akin to the analysis used for upstream effects in cases like Minnesota v. Clover Leaf Creamery (1981), and do not alone establish a “clearly excessive” burden. Absent discrimination or a direct attempt to control conduct occurring entirely outside California, the Dormant Commerce Clause does not authorize courts to invalidate this democratically enacted sales standard based on contested economic predictions.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Proposition 12 is an evenhanded in-state sales condition: it regulates what may be sold in California, not commerce occurring wholly outside the State, and its upstream effects on out-of-state producers are the kind of incidental market consequences typically assessed under Pike rather than condemned as per se “extraterritorial” regulation. Under Pike v. Bruce Church, Inc. (1970), petitioners would need to show burdens on interstate commerce that are clearly excessive in relation to the putative local benefits, and California’s asserted interests in consumer/moral preferences and health and safety associated with confinement practices qualify as cognizable local benefits for that analysis. Given the difficulty and administrability problems of having courts assign monetary weights to moral/consumer-welfare benefits versus industry compliance costs in an integrated national market, I would not invalidate a nondiscriminatory sales rule on this record absent discrimination or a more concrete showing of clearly excessive burden. Nothing in the federal statutory backdrop (including the Federal Meat Inspection Act, 21 U.S.C. § 601 et seq., or the Animal Health Protection Act, 7 U.S.C. § 8301 et seq.) clearly displaces state authority to set non-discriminatory conditions for products sold within the State.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Commerce Clause’s text grants Congress—not this Court—a power to regulate interstate commerce, and our “dormant” doctrine should not be expanded to invalidate an evenhanded in-state sales condition simply because it has upstream effects on out-of-state producers. Unlike the price-affirmation regimes in Healy v. Beer Institute (1989) and Brown-Forman Distillers v. N.Y. State Liquor Auth. (1986), Proposition 12 does not control the terms of out-of-state transactions or tie out-of-state prices to in-state mandates; it sets a rule for what may be sold in California. Petitioners’ request to strike the law under Pike v. Bruce Church (1970) would require courts to weigh moral and health-and-safety justifications against economic costs in a manner untethered to any administrable, text-based standard, and I would be reluctant to constitutionalize that policy choice absent discrimination or direct extraterritorial control. If uniform national standards are warranted, Congress remains free to act under Article I, § 8, cl. 3 (and statutes like the FMIA or AHPA), but in the absence of preemption, California may choose the characteristics of products sold within its borders.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Proposition 12 is an evenhanded in-state sales condition that applies to all pork sold in California regardless of origin, and the Dormant Commerce Clause generally permits States to regulate in-state sales even when those rules have significant upstream effects on out-of-state producers. Petitioners’ “extraterritoriality” theory would expand Dormant Commerce Clause doctrine beyond this Court’s traditional focus on discrimination and practical control of out-of-state transactions, and history and precedent counsel restraint before creating such a sweeping invalidation rule. Under Pike v. Bruce Church, the allegations of substantial compliance costs are relevant, but courts must be cautious about open-ended cost-benefit balancing where the asserted local interests include health/safety and moral/consumer concerns; at the pleading stage it is not clear the burdens are “clearly excessive” in relation to those putative benefits. Absent discrimination or a clearer showing of unworkable burdens, and given federal statutes like the FMIA do not expressly preempt this kind of sales condition, the law should be upheld.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The Commerce Clause’s text confers power on Congress, and the Court’s dormant Commerce Clause doctrine therefore operates as a limited, judge-made constraint principally aimed at discriminatory state laws; Proposition 12 is facially evenhanded because it regulates only what may be sold in California, regardless of origin. Petitioners’ “extraterritoriality” theory would extend that doctrine beyond its traditional application to price-control and price-affirmation statutes and would treat ordinary upstream compliance effects as per se unconstitutional, a move inconsistent with the Court’s approach of analyzing such incidental out-of-state effects under Pike v. Bruce Church, Inc. (1970). Under Pike, courts are ill-suited to second-guess California’s putative moral and health-and-safety interests or to weigh them against contested economic projections, and precedent counsels restraint in invalidating nondiscriminatory sales conditions absent discrimination or a clearly excessive burden. Nothing in the Animal Health Protection Act or the Federal Meat Inspection Act clearly preempts California’s sales condition here, reinforcing that the constitutional objection must rest on dormant Commerce Clause limits that are not met on these allegations.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Proposition 12 is an evenhanded in-state sales condition that applies to all pork sold in California regardless of origin, and the Dormant Commerce Clause does not bar a State from setting product-market access terms simply because they create upstream incentives for out-of-state producers. Petitioners’ “extraterritoriality” theory is too broad; where a nondiscriminatory law has incidental interstate effects, the proper framework is Pike v. Bruce Church, under which petitioners must plead and prove a substantial burden on interstate commerce that is clearly excessive relative to the putative local benefits. On this record, the asserted burdens—compliance and supply-chain adjustments driven by market participation—are not the kind of judicially manageable, clearly excessive burdens that justify invalidating a state law serving asserted local interests (including health/safety and moral consumer concerns). Absent discrimination or a direct regulation of wholly out-of-state transactions, Article I, § 8, cl. 3 does not authorize this Court to second-guess California’s policy choice through open-ended balancing.
